title: Working with the Quickfix List
summary: Chapter 4 teaches five quickfix-centric workflows for getting compiler, linter, grep, and test-runner output into Vim's error lists. It begins with compiler plugins, :make, and the :copen/:cnext family, then shows how Dispatch's :Make and :Dispatch commands make builds asynchronous and can infer or be told which compiler to use. The remaining tips cover ALE's asynchronous linting and its window-local location list, Grepper's asynchronous grep-alikes with per-tool settings, and vim-test's suite/file/nearest test commands plus its dispatch strategy for quickfix output.

commands.meaning: Run the program configured by 'makeprg' and load its output into the quickfix list; the chapter's starting point for capturing build errors.
commands.evidence: If you want to capture the output from an external program, you should reach for the :make command (:help :make).

commands.meaning: Activate the TypeScript compiler plugin, which sets buffer-local 'makeprg' and 'errorformat' together.
Open the quickfix window to inspect the errors captured by :make.
Jump to the first, previous, next, or last error in the quickfix list.
commands.evidence: You can traverse the list of errors using the commands: :cfirst, :cprev, :cnext, :clast.

commands.meaning: Dispatch's asynchronous :make: :Make runs the build in the foreground, :Make! sends it to the background.
commands.evidence: To summarize: the :Make command lets you run a build in the foreground, while the :Make! command lets you run a build in the background.

commands.meaning: Open the quickfix window on demand after the background build exits.
commands.evidence: The quickfix window doesn’t automatically open when the program exits, but you can open the quickfix window at your convenience using the :Copen command.

commands.meaning: Run a build tool through Dispatch, which selects a suitable compiler plugin before executing the command.
commands.evidence: The :Dispatch {cmd} command provides a one-step solution for setting up a compiler then executing a build tool.

commands.meaning: Force Dispatch to use the tslint compiler when the command (an npm script) hides the underlying tool.
Mappings to jump to the next and previous ALE warning.
commands.evidence: You can quickly jump forward and back between warnings using the ]w and [w mappings that you set up earlier.

commands.meaning: Manually trigger ALE linting; the book wires it to a <Leader>l mapping.
Traverse the window-local location list that ALE populates by default.
commands.evidence: That means you can use the :lfirst, :lprevious, :lnext, and :llast to traverse the warnings generated by linters.

commands.meaning: Run grep from Vim and load the matches into the quickfix list (synchronously).
Run grep asynchronously through Grepper; results populate the quickfix list when the job finishes.
Run the whole test suite with vim-test, which detects the test framework automatically.
Run the single test closest to the cursor.
commands.evidence: That’s where the :TestNearest command comes in.

concepts.name: Compiler plugins
concepts.evidence: The best way to ensure that you change both options simultaneously is by loading a compiler plugin.

concepts.name: ‘makeprg’ and ‘errorformat’ options
concepts.evidence: To use the :make command, you need to configure two options: ‘makeprg’ and ‘errorformat’.

concepts.name: Populating the quickfix list from compiler output
concepts.evidence: Vim executes the command specified by the ‘makeprg’ option, then populates the quickfix list using any output produced by that command.

concepts.name: Dispatch adapters
concepts.evidence: The Dispatch plugin supports several different adapters, allowing you to pick a strategy for running async commands that suits you.

concepts.name: Automatic compiler selection by matching ‘makeprg’
concepts.evidence: It works like this: For each compiler plugin in your runtimepath, the value of ‘makeprg’ is compared with your specified {cmd}.

concepts.name: g:dispatch_compilers dictionary
concepts.evidence: Or, you can teach dispatch how to choose the right compiler by adding to the g:dispatch_compilers dictionary.

concepts.name: Buffer-local b:dispatch default command
concepts.evidence: The b:dispatch variable is scoped to the buffer, which means you can specify a different default command for each buffer.

concepts.name: Quickfix list vs. location list scope
concepts.evidence: The quickfix list and location list provide similar functionality, but they differ in their scope.

concepts.name: Asynchronous linting with ALE
concepts.evidence: The ALE plugin runs linting tools asynchronously on your buffer.

concepts.name: g:ale_linters per-filetype configuration
concepts.evidence: To specify which linters you want to run for each filetype, use the g:ale_linters variable (:help g:ale_linters).

concepts.name: ‘grepprg’ and ‘grepformat’ for grep-alikes
concepts.evidence: By setting the ‘grepprg’ and ‘grepformat’ options, you can make the built-in :grep command call other tools besides grep.

concepts.name: vim-test dispatch strategy
concepts.evidence: With the dispatch strategy activated, vim-test executes the test-runner command using :Dispatch {cmd}.
